title: Cows that have drunk their last
theme: The boy’s thought: gifts that are spent and useless lead the giver to joyless worlds.

words.meaning: whose milk has been milked out

words.context: Śaṅkara: «प्रजननासमर्थाः जीर्णाः» — unable to calve, worn out

sandhi.type: visarga before t; n before s
sandhi.rule: Visarga becomes s before t, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः); the n of tān stands before s.
After ā the visarga is dropped before a voiced sound: P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि) and P. 8.3.22 (हलि सर्वेषाम्).
The visarga of saḥ is dropped before a consonant, P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि).

samasa.meaning: by whom the water has been drunk
by whom the grass has been eaten

morphology.note: Present active participle of dā (reduplicating class), nominative masculine, ‘giving’: the one who gives such cows goes to those worlds.
a- + nanda, ‘without joy’; Śaṅkara glosses anānandāḥ.

translation.literal: [Cows] that have drunk [their] water, eaten [their] grass, been milked of [their] milk, without strength — joyless, indeed, are those worlds; to them he goes, giving them.
translation.readable: ‘Cows that have drunk their last water, eaten their last grass, given their last milk, and can no longer calve — whoever gives such gifts goes to worlds without joy.’

anvaya: [याः] पीतोदकाः जग्धतृणाः दुग्धदोहाः निरिन्द्रियाः [गावः], ताः ददत् सः अनन्दाः नाम ते लोकाः [सन्ति] तान् गच्छति ॥
syntax: Four bahuvrīhi compounds describe the cows (the noun is understood); the second line is a nominal sentence (‘joyless are those worlds’) followed by ‘to them he goes, giving them’. The participle dadat (‘giving’) carries the condition.

ambiguities.note: The verse gives the content of the boy’s reflection (1.1.2 ends ‘he thought’). Raṅgarāmānuja closes it with «एवम् अमन्यत इत्यर्थः», ‘this is what he thought’.

ambiguities.topic: pītodakāḥ: past use or past need?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara takes the compounds as describing worn-out cows. Later Dvaita commentators on Madhva press the past participles: the cows have drunk and will drink no more — old cows near death.

beginner: Here we hear what the boy thinks as he watches. The cows being given away are old: they have drunk their last, eaten their last, given their last milk, and can no longer bear calves. A gift like that costs the giver nothing. The boy concludes that such giving does not lead to happiness; it leads to joyless worlds. This is the logic of the ritual his father believes in, taken seriously: if the gift is worthless, the reward will be worthless too. The boy is not rebelling against his father’s religion; he is holding it to its own standard. The verse also shows how the Upaniṣad works: from an ordinary scene it draws a question about what our actions really bring us.
analogy: Like donating only the clothes you would have thrown away anyway, and expecting gratitude for your generosity.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It describes worn-out cows and states that one who gives such gifts goes to ‘joyless worlds’. It is the content of the boy’s reflection.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: they are spent, useless cows — «निष्फला गाव इत्यर्थः» — and the giver goes to the worlds called joyless: «अनन्दाः अनानन्दाः असुखा नामेत्येतत्». Raṅgarāmānuja reads the verse as showing the shape of the boy’s faith: «श्रद्धाप्रकारमेव दर्शयति».

commentary.q: How does the Dvaita tradition read the scene?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva’s cited verse at the opening already names the fault: the father gave «ददौ गाश्च निरिन्द्रियाः», cows past use. Later Dvaita commentators on Madhva (Vyāsatīrtha, Vedeśatīrtha) press the past participles — the cows have drunk and will drink no more — and connect the ‘joyless worlds’ with the realm of darkness; they are not quoted here.

advaita.text: A gift of useless cows brings the giver to joyless worlds: «निष्फला गाव इत्यर्थः».

visistadvaita.text: The verse shows the form the boy’s faith took — «श्रद्धाप्रकारमेव दर्शयति» — and ends with what he thought: «एवम् अमन्यत इत्यर्थः».

dvaita.text: Madhva’s cited verse names the faulty gift: Uddālaka «ददौ गाश्च निरिन्द्रियाः», gave cows past use.

contemporary.text: Charity that disposes of what we no longer need can feel generous while costing nothing. The boy’s question is whether such giving changes anything in the giver. This is a modern reflection, not the text’s claim.

reflect.beginner: Is a gift that costs you nothing really a gift?
reflect.deeper: Why would the worth of what is given determine the worth of what is gained?
reflect.practice: Before your next gift or donation, ask what it costs you and whether that matters.
